My friend were discussing how the internet and streaming has been bad for music. While I have criticisms of the "studio system" and adore the DIY approach, I think in some respects the internet has had some limiting effects. There is certainly more potential to hear a variety of bands but more isn't necessarily better.

It's the question of exposure vs profit. You could successfully put one song on Youtube [exposure] and include a link to a retailer which sells the whole album [profit]. But putting the whole album on Spotify and expecting to get both those things is probably, unless you are wildly (I mean chart-topper wildly) popular, not going to happen.

For a solo artist to earn the U.S. monthly minimum wage of $1,160, they must sell/achieve:

  • 143 self-pressed CDs

  • 1,229 itunes/napster album downloads

  • 3,871 retail album CDs

  • 12,399 itunes/amazon track downloads

  • 1,546,667 last. fm streams

  • 4,053,110 spotify streams

To read more on a similar subject, I found this info through a link from this fascinating article by David Byrne: quote: "The boom in digital streaming may generate profits for record labels and free content for consumers, but it spells disaster for today's artists across the creative industries."

Edit: The link is to an older infogram. The Guardian did a new one this year, Check it out here. Surprisingly, it actually seems more possible, both in terms of self-pressed CDs to spotify streams, to make that monthly minimum wage today than it did five years ago.
Or. They can rent out a venue for a few hundred bucks, sell tickets for $15 bucks and make way more than that. Source: This is how you make money as a musician.
